lines.note: Continues a Japanese example from the preceding page: tsukuri-daite mono wo yuu, saying something invented or fabricated. The Portuguese begins the explanation as saying something; the full final couſa is printed, with no terminal hyphen.
Completes the fabricated-speech gloss: feigning it or inventing it oneself. Both object pronouns remain attached as printed; this is the continuation of the preceding example.
Tsukuri-monogatari is invented or fictitious discourse. The native scan supports monogatari and fingida, correcting OCR monogarari and ſingida; fa- begins the Portuguese adjective on the next row.
Completes fabulosa, giving the alternative description of a fictional or fabulous account. This short printed continuation remains a separate body line.
Tsukuri-naoshi, -su, -oita means remaking or correcting what was made badly. The historical principal parts and the divided eſ- are retained rather than regularized.

Completes the explanation as what is badly made. Expected Portuguese would have està across the break, but the surviving second glyph looks like dotted i at enlargement; the supplied ti is retained as a damaged or anomalous printed reading rather than silently emended.
Tsukuri-nashi means making or giving form to something. The printed ita principal part is retained; the gloss pairs fazer with dar forma, linked by Latin l, meaning or.
Completes dar forma a alguma cousa: giving shape to an object. The damaged internal strokes do not justify changing the aligned algũa reading.

Tsukuri-tate is erecting or constructing. The headword is heavily abraded through curit; surviving strokes and the building gloss support Tçucuritate, corroborated by the attributed NINJAL index. The scan leaves no secure comma between uru and eta, so its absence is preserved.
Completes the preceding construction gloss with buildings or structures. Fabricas here refers to constructed works, without requiring the modern industrial sense of factories.
Tsukuri-warai is an affected or feigned laugh, directly matched by riso fingido. The worn medial ri is recovered from the surviving type and headword context, not the malformed OCR Tçucunuarai.

Tsukuri-yamai, alternatively sakubyoo, is a feigned illness. The weak initial in the synonym is long ſ rather than capital I; NINJAL independently corroborates sakubyoo after the scan reading. The caron over the final o is preserved.

Tsukuri-zame is an artificial imitation of the sharkskin-like covering described below. The weak medial ri replaces OCR ui; the Portuguese says that the material is made artificially in imitation of something.

runs.text: maneira de pelle de lica que poem os Iapões nos

lines.note: The imitation resembles the lica skin that Japanese people place on sword handles. The scan supports lica as printed; it is not silently replaced by the expected modern fish-name spelling lixa.
Completes the object description: the handles of catanas. The final abbreviation is &c., with c rather than the OCR e, and belongs to the Portuguese explanation.
Tsukuroi, -roo, -oota means repairing or putting in order, with a second sense of adorning. Concertar supplies the missing c in OCR Conertar; both long-o marks are visibly circumflexes.

runs.text: ¶ Itẽ, Refazer, ou tornar a concertar algũa

lines.note: Adds the sense of remaking or repairing something again. The abbreviation Itẽ is retained, and the object introduced by algũa continues onto the following line.

runs.text: couſa, ou obra que està danada, quebrada, &c.

lines.note: Completes the repair sense: an object or work that is damaged or broken. The printed danada and grave-marked està remain historical forms; the supplied st treatment is preserved because the tall stroke belongs to a difficult joined type.
Mi wo tsukuroo means putting oneself in good order or adorning oneself. The visible paragraph marker omitted by OCR is restored; or- starts ornarse on the next physical row.
Completes ornarse, then gives kizu wo tsukuroo, treating a wound. The object algũa ferida is divided at al- and continues below.

runs.text: gũa ferida. ¶ Item, Tomar o beneplacito

lines.note: Completes the wound example, then adds winning another person’s approval or goodwill. Beneplacito identifies the social sense that the following Japanese example illustrates.

runs.text: de alguem, l, ganharlhe a vontade. Vt,

lines.note: The sense is gaining someone’s good will; the scan reads ganharlhe a vontade, correcting the OCR’s fused ganharlhoa. Fito- begins hito no kigen wo tsukuroo on the next row.

Completes hito no kigen wo tsukuroo, conciliating someone or attending to their mood. The next example is uma wo tsukuroo, tending a horse: the native letter after a has the open top and bottom join of u, correcting OCR Vmano. The initial V retains its supplied mixed typeface but remains part of the Japanese example.

runs.text: Sangrar os caualos, cortar lheſas vnhas, &

lines.note: Completes the horse-care example: bleed the horses and trim their hooves. Sangrar is chosen from the surviving types and the treatment context; the first vowel is abraded, while no secure i-dot supports OCR Singrar. The compressed lheſas spacing is retained.

runs.text: curalos pera que não ſe danem os pès, &c.

lines.note: Continues the horse-care gloss: tend them so that their feet are not damaged. The grave in pès and the historical pera remain as printed.

Zashiki or furumai wo tori-tsukuroo concerns arranging a reception room or banquet. Latin l coordinates the two alternative Japanese objects, while tori-tsukuroo supplies the action of putting them in order.

runs.text: Aparelhar, & concertar bem o zaxiqui, con-

lines.note: The Portuguese explains preparing and putting the zashiki in good order; zaxiqui is a Japanese word embedded within the explanation. The visible separation bem o corrects bemo, and con- begins convite below.
Completes convite, a banquet or entertainment, before uchiwa wo tsukuroo, restoring harmony within a group. Concer- begins the repair metaphor in the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: tar a amizade dalgũs de maneira que não que-

lines.note: Completes concertar a amizade: repairing relations among people so that the friendship does not break entirely. The abbreviated nasal in dalgũs remains unexpanded.

runs.text: bre de todo, ou ſetorne a ſoldar como primeiro.

lines.note: Completes quebre, then explains restoring or welding the friendship together as before. The very weak r in bre is selected from the surviving shoulder and the divided quebrar construction; the cropped impression is i-like, so this chosen reading remains a caveat.
Tori ga hazukuroi, alternatively hanezukuroi wo, introduces a bird’s grooming or preening. The long compounds retain their printed doubled z and continue with suru on the next row.

Suru completes the bird-preening example. The Portuguese describes a bird picking or grooming itself and arranging its feathers; the close Eſpinicarſe types are joined rather than preserving the OCR’s inserted space.

Tsukushi means exhausting or using up completely. The scan confirms the printed abbreviated principal part u, although the following examples have tsukusu; this apparent paradigm anomaly is preserved rather than supplied with an s.

Kokoro wo tsukusu means devoting one’s whole care or effort. The Portuguese cuidado is divided after cuida-; its initial T retains the supplied roman type beside italic er, supported by comparison with the nearby Japanese capital T.

runs.text: do, ou por mu ta diligencia com aflição.

lines.note: Completes cuidado and adds diligent effort accompanied by anxiety or distress. Aflição is visible, correcting OCR aſtição. The space in mu ta is retained because the expected i of muita is not securely visible in the abraded gap.
Yomi-tsukusu is reading everything, leaving nothing unread. The Portuguese makes the exhaustive sense explicit and confirms the verb form rather than an unrelated final syllable.
Mono wo kui-tsukusu means eating everything up. Te- at the right begins a new example, te wo tsukusu, which carries over to the next physical line.
Completes te wo tsukusu, applying every means or skill to a task. The Portuguese describes taking pains over doing something; Eſmerarſe is visibly contiguous, and cou- continues below.

runs.text: ſa, ou vſar de todas as artes, ou lições que hum

lines.note: Completes cousa, then explains using all the arts or lessons one has learned. The long ſ in vſar corrects OCR vfar; this is the historical spelling of usar.
Completes the learned-skills explanation with fencing as an example. Fix- is roman Japanese, beginning the term hissei on the next row, and remains outside the preceding italic Portuguese gloss.
Fix- plus xei forms hissei, the force or skill of the brush; hissei wo tsukusu is exerting that skill fully. The Portuguese applies it to writing and continues below.
Completes the brush-skill example: writing a fine hand or painting. The short continuation closes this sense of tsukusu before the next independent headword.
Tsukue is a writing desk or table, described as a banco de escrever. The native form Tçucuye replaces OCR Tçuenye and is corroborated by NINJAL after inspection.
Tsukuzukuto is an adverb for close or careful attention. The two z types are retained from the headword and repeated example, replacing malformed OCR Tçucuezucuto.
Completes the adverbial gloss and begins tsukuzukuto miru, looking intently; Latin l supplies the alternative construction with shian suru below.
Shian suru gives the reflective alternative, considering something carefully. The Portuguese conſiderar, visibly with i after long ſ, corrects OCR conſaderar.
Atentamente completes the explanation of careful looking or reflection. This is the final body row of column 1, with no omitted lower continuation in the native scan.

runs.text: Hũa erua q̃ nace no Nigua-

lines.note: Tsukuzukushi is described as an herb growing in the second month and resembling a Japanese writing brush. The native headword corrects OCR Tçueuzucuxi; Nigua- begins the Japanese month-name Nigwachi embedded in the Portuguese gloss.
Chi completes Nigwachi, the second month in the Japanese calendar. The plant is compared to a Japanese pen or writing brush; this is a continuation of the botanical description, not a new headword.

Tsuudat is paraphrased by toori tassuru, passing through or penetrating. The vowel is u with a caron and the final checked t is preserved; the native scan supports the mixed long-and-short s pair in taſsuru.
Completes a theological illustration of penetration, as by glorified bodies. A second sense then applies penetration to understanding things intellectually.

runs.text: couſas com grande lume do entendimento, &

lines.note: The intellectual sense involves penetrating matters through great light of understanding. Entendimento has a clear m sequence and corrects OCR entendinento.
Completes the intellectual gloss with knowledge like that of angels. The final S is the written-language usage label, retained in the supplied italic treatment.
Tsuda-tsuda means in little pieces. The example begins with the repeated expression and divides at Tçuda-; the spelling is retained without substituting modern zuta-zuta.
Completes tsuda-tsuda ni kiri-hanasu, cutting apart into small pieces. The printed qiri and long ſ of fanaſu agree with the Japanese verb structure and the cutting gloss.

runs.text: pedacinhos. Posto que na pratica ordinariamen

lines.note: Completes the small-pieces translation, then comments on the form commonly used in speech. Ordinariamen continues as te below, but the right edge shows no printed terminal hyphen.

Completes ordinariamente and reports the spoken form zuda-zuda, which the dictionary calls less proper. Zzudazzuda is Japanese cited within a Portuguese explanation, while the Latin minùs propriè retains its accents.
Tsudoi, -doo, -oota describes people coming together one after another. The two principal-part accents are circumflexes, and hũs is the printed abbreviation in the Portuguese gloss.
Completes the first explanation and gives hito ga mairi-tsudoo, people coming and gathering. Mui- begins muita in the Portuguese translation below.
Completes muita gente, specifying people arriving one after another. The short row closes the tsudou entry before the distinct word for spit.

Tsuhaki is followed by the preferable form tsubaki, meaning spit or saliva in this entry. Latin potiùs supplies the preference; the Portuguese Cuſpo prevents confusion with the homophonous tree-name tsubaki.
Tsuuhou is explained as a rule or something ordinary. The scan gives couſa and the divided repeated form Tçǔ-, correcting OCR coaſa and Tgǔ-; both Japanese vowel marks are retained.
Completes tsuuhou no hito de nai, saying that someone is no ordinary person. The line begins with lowercase f, not the OCR capital F; the Portuguese follows the same negative evaluation.
Adds that the person is not just anybody. This completes the non-ordinary-person example and is not a separate lexical entry.
Tsuuhouna is the adjectival form, exemplified by tsuuhouna hito, an ordinary person. The caroned u restores the malformed OCR headword Tçhfǒna; Ho- begins homem below.
Mem completes homem, translating tsuuhouna hito as an ordinary person. It is the continuation of the previous example, not another entry.

runs.text: Iunturas dos membros, ou dos oſſos, ẽ-

lines.note: Tsugai denotes joints of the limbs or bones and, next, hinges. The scan has oſſos followed by punctuation, not OCR oſſosr; the abbreviated ẽ- begins engonços on the next row.
Completes engonços, then gives tsugai ga hanareta, a joint coming apart or becoming dislocated. Deſ- is the printed beginning of the Portuguese explanation below.

runs.text: liarſe, ou deſengonçarſe algũa couſa da outra.

lines.note: Completes desliarse and explains one thing separating or becoming unhinged from another. The historical liar-based form is retained without inserting a modern g.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Conjunção, ou enſejo.

lines.note: Adds a figurative sense: a conjunction of circumstances or an opportunity. Conjunção is visible, correcting OCR Contunção; per met. is retained as the printed figurative-use abbreviation.

Tsugai wo mite moosoozu means that the speaker will speak when an opportunity arises. The prospective ending has a clearly grave-marked final u; the second caron is faint but retained from the surviving mark and aligned reading.
Completes conjunção and the future-tense explanation: on seeing an opportunity, I shall speak. Falarei supports the prospective reading of the preceding Japanese form.
Tsugai, -oo, -oota is joining or attaching two things. The principal-part o marks are visibly carons and are not assimilated to the circumflexes of tsudou earlier in the column.

runs.text: como portas comengonços, biǒbus que ſe dobrão,

lines.note: Examples are doors with hinges and folding byoobu screens. The mark in biǒbus is a clear caron, contrasting with the tilde in dobrão on the same row; the Portuguese plural s remains on the Japanese term. Printed comengonços is retained without inserting a space.
Ashi wo tsugoote nuru describes sleeping with feet interlocked. The historical contracted te-form and nuru are retained; Dormi- begins the Portuguese infinitive below.

runs.text: rem dous com os pès trauados hum com outro.

lines.note: Completes dormirem: two people sleep with their feet linked together. The grave-marked pès and historical trauados are preserved rather than modernized.
Tori no hitotsugai is one pair of birds. The scan supports fitotçugai, correcting OCR fitorçugai; paßa- continues the Portuguese bird noun below.
Completes passaros and specifies a male-and-female pair. Femea corrects the extraneous r in OCR fermea; hato hitotsugai begins the next example, a pair of pigeons or doves.

runs.text: Hum par de rolas, ou pombas.

lines.note: Gai completes hato hitotsugai. The Portuguese gives a pair of turtledoves or pigeons, illustrating the pairing sense of tsugai.
Tsugai-gomono denotes a pair of attendants walking in front. The Portuguese states two servants, and their position relative to a horse or litter continues below.

runs.text: do caualo, ou do Coxi de hũa librè juntos.

lines.note: The paired attendants precede a horse or koshi litter and wear the same livery. Coxi is embedded Japanese within Portuguese; the native grave in librè replaces OCR librẽ, and the narrow but visible word separation before juntos is retained.

runs.text: Aquelle nô, ou juntura onde ſe a-

lines.note: Tsugaime is the knot or joint where two things meet. The worn first l in Aquelle retains a high stem remnant, so the OCR gap is closed and both l types preserved; nô has a visible circumflex, not a grave.
Completes ajuntão and explains joining or binding two objects. The printed lião is retained as a historical spelling without supplying a g.

Tsuge is a revelation, message, or announcement. Gotçu- begins go-tsuge, the honorific form, across the line break; the locally upright Vt retains the supplied typeface rather than receiving an automatic italic conversion.

Completes go-tsuge, here a revelation from heaven or from the Buddha. Fotoqe is visibly roman within the italic Portuguese explanation; the final &c. is wholly italic, correcting the OCR’s isolated roman c.
Tsuge, -uru, -eta means revealing, informing, or announcing. The scan shows the i of auiſar before long ſ, correcting OCR auſſar.

Completes the announcement gloss and begins uguisu kitatte haru wo tsuguru: the uguisu comes and announces spring. The initial V is preserved in the supplied mixed typeface; it belongs to the Japanese bird-name, not to the Portuguese apparatus.

runs.text: Vindo o Rouxinol traz nouas da pri-

lines.note: Guru completes the historical terminal tsuguru. The Portuguese renders the bird as Rouxinol and says that its arrival brings news of spring; pri- continues below.
Completes prima vera, spring, retaining the printed internal space. This closes the bird-arrival example before the homophonous tree-name tsuge.

Tsuge, alternatively tsuge no ki, is identified simply as a tree of that name. The native types read aßicha-, with the ß-like sort and no extra t; the closely set words and physical division are preserved.
Mada completes chamada after aßicha-, meaning a tree so called. No additional botanical identification is asserted by this brief gloss.
Tsuge-shirase means making something known or giving notice. The printed abbreviated ſuru principal part remains as supplied, and the close Portuguese aſaber spelling is retained.
Denunciar completes the alternative gloss of announcing or reporting. The short continuation is a genuine body row immediately before tsugi.

runs.text: Remendo, ou pedaço que ſe acrecen

lines.note: Tsugi is a patch or an added piece. The native initial T omitted by OCR is restored; acrecen continues as ta at the opening of f0484, while the separate bottom-right ta. is a catchword. No terminal hyphen is visible at this body-row edge.
